summary: Describes HTTP Live Streaming, a protocol for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data. It specifies the file data format and the actions of servers and clients. It describes version 7 of the protocol and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP Live Streaming delivers video as a series of short files over ordinary web requests. A playlist file names the pieces and how long they are, and a second playlist offers the same content at several quality levels. The player picks a level to match the connection it has at the moment, so the picture keeps going when the network slows down.

questions: how to adapt video quality in streaming
subtitle: How a video stream is cut into files and described by a playlist, so the viewer can change quality without stopping.

tldr.problem: Delivering continuous video over the Internet means coping with a network whose capacity changes, and with viewers on different connections. Serving one fixed file to everyone means either stalling or wasting bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP Live Streaming cuts the media into short segments and publishes a plain-text playlist that lists them. A second playlist, the master playlist, lists several versions of the same content at different bit rates, and the client switches between them as conditions change.
tldr.outcome: The result is version 7 of the protocol, with rules for the playlist files, the segment formats, what the server must publish and what the client must do, and a scheme for encrypting segments.

facts.label: Target duration in the example playlist

today: RFC 8216 is an Informational document published in August 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it describes version 7 of the protocol. The security considerations of the HTTP specification it builds on are in RFC 7230.

sections.title: What HTTP Live Streaming Does
sections.content:
HTTP Live Streaming provides a reliable, cost-effective means of delivering continuous and long-form video over the Internet. It allows a receiver to adapt the bit rate of the media to the current network conditions in order to maintain uninterrupted playback at the best possible quality. It supports interstitial content boundaries, provides a flexible framework for media encryption, can efficiently offer multiple renditions of the same content such as audio translations, and offers compatibility with large-scale HTTP caching infrastructure to support delivery to large audiences.

Since the Internet-Draft was first posted in 2009, HTTP Live Streaming has been implemented and deployed by a wide array of content producers, tools vendors, distributors and device manufacturers, and the protocol has been refined by extensive review and discussion with a variety of media streaming implementors. The purpose of the document is to facilitate interoperability between implementations by describing the media transmission protocol, and it describes version 7 of the protocol.

A multimedia presentation is specified by a URI to a playlist. A playlist is either a media playlist or a master playlist, and both are UTF-8 text files containing URIs and descriptive tags. A media playlist contains a list of media segments which, played sequentially, play the presentation. To play it, the client first downloads the playlist and then downloads and plays each media segment declared within it, reloading the playlist to discover any added segments. Data should be carried over HTTP, but a URI can in general specify any protocol that can reliably transfer the specified resource on demand.

A more complex presentation is described by a master playlist, which provides a set of variant streams, each describing a different version of the same content. A variant stream includes a media playlist that specifies media encoded at a particular bit rate, in a particular format, and at a particular resolution for media containing video. A variant stream can also specify a set of renditions, which are alternate versions of the content such as audio produced in different languages or video recorded from different camera angles. Clients should switch between variant streams to adapt to network conditions, and should choose renditions based on user preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to serve video as ordinary web files that a plain web server can deliver, so that the huge caching systems built for the web can carry a stream to a large audience. Because the files are separate, the player can drop to a lower quality version when the connection gets slow and go back up when it improves, without the viewer noticing a restart.

sections.title: Media Segments and Their Formats
sections.content:
A media playlist contains a series of media segments that make up the overall presentation. A media segment is specified by a URI and optionally a byte range, and its duration is indicated in the playlist by its EXTINF tag.

Each segment in a media playlist has a unique integer media sequence number. The number of the first segment is either zero or declared in the playlist, and the number of every other segment is one more than the segment before it. Each segment must carry the continuation of the encoded bitstream from the end of the segment with the previous media sequence number, where values in a series such as timestamps and continuity counters must continue uninterrupted. The only exceptions are the first media segment ever to appear in a media playlist and segments explicitly signalled as discontinuities, because unmarked media discontinuities can trigger playback errors. Any segment containing video should include enough information to initialize a video decoder and decode a continuous set of frames that includes the final frame in the segment; for example, a segment containing H.264 video should contain an Instantaneous Decoding Refresh, and frames before the first one will be downloaded but possibly discarded.

Some media formats need a common sequence of bytes to initialize a parser before a segment can be parsed. That sequence is called the media initialization section, it can be specified by an EXT-X-MAP tag, and it must not contain sample data. The document defines four segment formats.

MPEG-2 Transport Streams have a media initialization section made of a Program Association Table followed by a Program Map Table. A transport stream segment must contain a single MPEG-2 program, because playback of multi-program transport streams is not defined, and each segment must contain a PAT and a PMT or have an EXT-X-MAP tag applied to it.

Fragmented MPEG-4 differs from a regular MPEG-4 file in that a fragment consists of a Movie Fragment Box containing a subset of the sample table, and a Media Data Box containing those samples, while a Movie Box is still needed for initialization. The media initialization section for such a segment must contain a File Type Box with a brand compatible with iso6 or higher, followed by a Movie Box, and the Movie Box must contain a Track Box for every Track Fragment Box in the segment with a matching track identifier. Every Track Fragment Box must contain a Track Fragment Decode Time Box, and each fMP4 segment in a media playlist must have an EXT-X-MAP tag applied to it.

Packed Audio contains encoded audio samples and ID3 tags simply packed together with minimal framing and no per-sample timestamps. The supported formats are Advanced Audio Coding with ADTS framing, MP3, AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3. Each packed audio segment must signal the timestamp of its first sample with an ID3 Private frame tag at the beginning of the segment, and clients should not play packed audio segments without it.

WebVTT segments carry subtitles. Each must contain all the subtitle cues intended to be displayed during the period the segment covers, and must either start with a WebVTT header or have an EXT-X-MAP tag applied to it. To synchronise timestamps between the audio and video and the subtitles, an X-TIMESTAMP-MAP metadata header should be added to each WebVTT header, mapping the cue timestamps to the MPEG-2 timestamps used in the other renditions of the variant stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of the stream is a separate file, and the pieces have to fit together: the timestamps and counters continue across the boundary, and the file starts with enough information for the player to start decoding it. Four container formats are allowed, and each has its own rule about how the player gets the information it needs before the first frame.

sections.title: The Playlist File Format
sections.content:
The playlist files are derived from the M3U playlist file format and inherit two tags from it, EXTM3U and EXTINF. In the specification of tag syntax, a string enclosed in angle brackets identifies a tag parameter; if a parameter is further surrounded by square brackets it is optional, otherwise it is required.

Each playlist file must be identifiable either by the path component of its URI or by HTTP Content-Type. In the first case the path must end with either .m3u8 or .m3u; in the second the content type must be application/vnd.apple.mpegurl or audio/mpegurl. Clients should refuse to parse playlists that are not so identified.

Playlist files must be encoded in UTF-8 and must not contain a Byte Order Mark, and must not contain UTF-8 control characters other than carriage return and line feed. All character sequences must be normalised according to Unicode normalization form NFC. Lines are terminated by a single line feed or a carriage return followed by a line feed, and each line is a URI, is blank, or starts with the character '#'. Blank lines are ignored and whitespace must not be present except where it is explicitly specified. Lines starting with '#' are either comments or tags; tags begin with #EXT, they are case sensitive, and all other lines starting with '#' are comments and should be ignored.

A playlist is a media playlist if all URI lines identify media segments, and a master playlist if all URI lines identify media playlists. A playlist must be one or the other, and all other playlists are invalid. A URI in a playlist may be relative, in which case it is relative to the URI of the playlist that contains it. The duration of a media playlist is the sum of the durations of its media segments.

The bit rates the protocol talks about are defined in terms of the segments. The segment bit rate of a media segment is its size divided by its EXTINF duration, which includes container overhead but not the overhead of the delivery system such as HTTP, TCP or IP headers. The peak segment bit rate of a media playlist is the largest bit rate of any contiguous set of segments whose total duration is between 0.5 and 1.5 times the target duration. The average segment bit rate is the sum of the sizes of every segment divided by the playlist duration.
sections.plainLanguage: A playlist is an ordinary text file of lines, most of them addresses. Lines that start with a hash are either tags that carry information or comments to be ignored. The file must be plain UTF-8 text with no odd control characters, and it must make clear which kind of playlist it is, either from its name ending in .m3u8 or from the content type the server sends.

sections.title: What the Server and the Client Must Do
sections.content:
The server must divide the source media into individual media segments whose duration is less than or equal to a constant target duration, because segments that are longer than the planned target duration can trigger playback stalls and other errors. It should try to divide the source media at points that support effective decode, for example on packet and key frame boundaries, and it must create a URI for every segment that enables clients to obtain the segment data. Any media segment specified in a playlist loaded by a client must be available for immediate download, or playback errors can occur.

The server must not change the media playlist file except to append lines to it, to remove media segment URIs from the playlist in the order that they appear along with any tags that apply only to those segments, to increment the value of the EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE or EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY-SEQUENCE tags, or to add an EXT-X-ENDLIST tag. Changes must be made atomically from the point of view of the clients. If segments are to be removed, the playlist must contain an EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE tag whose value is incremented by one for every segment removed, and segments must be removed in the order in which they appear, otherwise client playback can malfunction. The server must not remove a segment from a playlist without an EXT-X-ENDLIST tag if that would leave a playlist whose duration is less than three times the target duration, because that can trigger playback stalls.

Media segments may be encrypted. Every encrypted segment must have an EXT-X-KEY tag applied to it with a URI the client can use to obtain a key file containing the decryption key, and a server may offer several ways to retrieve the same key by providing multiple EXT-X-KEY tags with different KEYFORMAT attribute values. A key file holds the cipher key, and AES-128 encryption uses 16-octet keys. The key file itself may be fetched over HTTP, and the delivery of these keys should be secured by a mechanism such as HTTP over TLS in conjunction with a secure realm or a session token.

On the client side, the client must determine the next media segment to load every time a media playlist is loaded or reloaded, and in order to play the presentation normally the next segment is the one with the lowest media sequence number greater than that of the last segment loaded. The client must periodically reload a media playlist to learn what media is currently available, unless it is a VOD playlist, or an EVENT playlist that also carries the end list tag, and it must not reload more frequently than specified, to limit the collective load on the server. After reloading, the client should verify that each segment has the same URI, and byte range if specified, as the segment with the same media sequence number in the previous playlist, and should halt playback if it does not, because that normally indicates a server error. Clients should switch between variant streams as network conditions change, and should not reload the playlists of variant streams they are not playing.
sections.plainLanguage: The server cuts the video into short pieces and publishes a list that it then keeps updating by appending. It is not allowed to rewrite the list in any other way, because a client that reloads it mid-stream must be able to trust what it sees. The client reloads the list on a timer, works out which piece comes next, and switches to a different quality level when it needs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the protocol generally uses HTTP to transfer data, most of the same security considerations apply as for HTTP itself.

Media file parsers are typically subject to fuzzing attacks, so implementors should pay particular attention to the code that parses data received from a server and ensure that all possible inputs are handled correctly. Playlist files contain URIs, which clients use to make network requests of arbitrary entities, and clients should range-check responses to prevent buffer overflows.

Apart from URL resolution, the format does not employ any form of active content. Clients should limit each playback session to a reasonable number of concurrent downloads, for example four, to avoid contributing to denial-of-service attacks. HTTP requests often include session state in cookies, which may contain private user data, so implementations must follow the cookie restriction and expiry rules to protect themselves from attack. Finally, encryption keys are specified by URI, and the delivery of these keys should be secured by a mechanism such as HTTP over TLS in conjunction with a secure realm or a session token.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the risk comes from the ordinary risks of fetching files over HTTP: a parser that crashes on a malformed file, a playlist that points the player at a server it should not talk to, or a key fetched without protection. The document asks for a limit on how many things a player downloads at once, so that a stream is not used to overwhelm a server.

items.title: MPEG-2 Transport Streams
items.text: Each segment must carry a PAT and a PMT, or have an EXT-X-MAP tag applied to it.

items.title: Fragmented MPEG-4
items.text: Each fMP4 segment must have an EXT-X-MAP tag applied to it, and a Track Fragment Decode Time Box.

items.title: Packed Audio
items.text: Samples and ID3 tags packed together, with the first sample's timestamp in an ID3 PRIV tag.

items.title: WebVTT
items.text: Subtitle cues, with an X-TIMESTAMP-MAP header to line them up with the other renditions.

cells: Must divide the source into segments no longer than the target duration
Must not start less than three target durations from the end of a live playlist
May only append lines, remove segment URIs in order, raise the sequence numbers, or add EXT-X-ENDLIST
Must reload periodically, waiting at least one target duration after a change
Publishes the variant streams and their bandwidth attributes
Switches between variant streams as network conditions change
Publishes an EXT-X-KEY tag for each encrypted segment
Fetches the key file and decrypts the segment it applies to
